note: Every threshold cites a source card in `sources`. `quote` is verbatim from the held book and is machine-checked against the PDF by tests/landscape/rules/test_source_quotes.py (skipped where the book is absent). Status `sourced` = verbatim passage read on the page; `policy` = ours, stated as ours; `unverified` = named but passage not read. Time-Saver is North American practice (units converted by the book); Metric Handbook is UK. No jurisdiction pack: this is guidance, not code compliance.

sources.document: Harris & Dines, Time-Saver Standards for Landscape Architecture
sources.locator: p. 340-5, 3.1 Pathway Width and Slope Criteria
sources.quote: a 600 mm (24 in) width for each pedestrian is necessary, which suggests a minimum pathway width of 1 200 mm (4 ft) for public walkways
sources.value: 600 mm per pedestrian; 1 200 mm minimum for a public walkway
sources.note: Public walkways. Applied to the garden's main route by analogy (two people abreast); a 600 mm single-file secondary path follows from the same 600 mm-per-pedestrian figure.

sources.document: Harris & Dines, Time-Saver Standards for Landscape Architecture
sources.quote: 2R + T = 650 to 675 mm (26 to 27 in) where R = riser T = tread
sources.value: 2R + G = 650 to 675 mm
sources.note: Outdoor stairways.

sources.document: Harris & Dines, Time-Saver Standards for Landscape Architecture
sources.quote: Risers for outdoor stairways should be a minimum of 115 mm (4.5 in) and a maximum of 150 mm (6 in) . Under utilitarian circumstances a 175 (7 in) riser may be considered
sources.value: riser 115-150 mm; 175 mm only utilitarian

sources.document: Harris & Dines, Time-Saver Standards for Landscape Architecture
sources.quote: Single steps in a walkway are very dangerous and should never be specified. At least two steps, but preferably three, should be specified, and their presence should be announced conspicuously with railings, plantings, or lighting
sources.value: at least 2 steps (3 preferred); announce them conspicuously
sources.note: Directly relevant to the flush-with-the-ground brief: any level change must be announced.

sources.document: Harris & Dines, Time-Saver Standards for Landscape Architecture
sources.quote: Treads should be pitched downgrade 2 percent for drainage
sources.value: tread pitch 2 % downgrade

sources.document: Harris & Dines, Time-Saver Standards for Landscape Architecture
sources.quote: Minimum width for stairways should be 1 500 mm (60 in) for public spaces and 1 050 mm (42 in) for private spaces
sources.value: private stair width >= 1 050 mm

sources.document: Harris & Dines, Time-Saver Standards for Landscape Architecture
sources.quote: Heights between stair landings should be a maximum of 1 500 mm (5 ft)
sources.value: rise between landings <= 1 500 mm

sources.document: Harris & Dines, Time-Saver Standards for Landscape Architecture
sources.quote: Seatwalls are typically 400 to 450 mm (16 to 18 in) wide and between 350 and 450 mm (14 and 18 in) in height
sources.value: seat wall width 400-450 mm, height 350-450 mm
sources.note: 'Typically': a typical range, not a legal limit.

sources.document: Harris & Dines, Time-Saver Standards for Landscape Architecture
sources.locator: p. 210-3, 2.1 Human Spatial Settings and Figure 210-3
sources.quote: a 3 000 x 3 000 mm (10 x 10 ft) dining room when placed on a patio setting typically requires a 3 600 x 3 600 mm or 3 600 x 4 500 mm (12 x 12 ft or 12 x 15 ft) exterior floor area
sources.value: outdoor dining space 40-60 % greater than indoor
sources.note: Figure 210-3 (page image read, 2026-11-22): round table with 4 chairs inside a 4 200 mm diameter circle, plus a 1 200 mm circulation strip (overall 3 600 x 4 800 mm). Per-seat area 3.46 m2 = pi*2.1^2/4; with the strip 4.32 m2 = 3.6*4.8/4. The figure shows 4 seats; the per-seat value is DERIVED by us from the drawing, not printed.

sources.document: Harris & Dines, Time-Saver Standards for Landscape Architecture
sources.quote: Patio dining requirements . Circulation space should be factored into spatial design
sources.value: 4 200 mm dia. circle around a 4-seat table; 1 200 mm circulation strip
sources.note: Dimensions read from the figure image (FIG), not from text.

sources.document: DeChiara, Panero & Zelnik, Time-Saver Standards for Interior Design and Space Planning
sources.quote: A minimum of 48 in, or 121.9 cm, is suggested from the edge of the table to the wall or nearest obstruction
sources.value: 1 219 mm table edge to wall or obstruction
sources.note: Indoor conference table, used only to corroborate the 1 200 mm strip of Figure 210-3. Outdoors needs more space (TS 210-3), so this is a floor, not a target.

sources.document: Harris & Dines, Time-Saver Standards for Landscape Architecture
sources.quote: A clear, level ground space around fire rings and pedestal grills should be at least 900 mm (36 in) on all sides, with 1 200 mm (48 in) being recommended
sources.value: clear level ground >= 900 mm all sides; 1 200 mm recommended
sources.note: Accessible-camping context: it is a ground-space figure for use, not a fire-safety clearance to combustibles. Clearance to facade and planting follows the product's instructions (brief).

sources.document: Harris & Dines, Time-Saver Standards for Landscape Architecture
sources.quote: A fire ring is optional, but if included it should be at least 1 800 mm (6 ft) in diameter and 1 500 mm (5 ft) from the nearest seated audience
sources.value: 1 500 mm fire ring to nearest seated person
sources.note: Council-ring (camp amphitheatre) context with a >= 1 800 mm ring: a larger open fire than a domestic pit. Used as a warning, not a limit.

sources.document: Harris & Dines, Time-Saver Standards for Landscape Architecture
sources.locator: p. 530-15, 5.4 Cross-Sectional Configuration, Clearance from Displays
sources.quote: Where pool edges are flush with the paving, an additional margin of safety should be obtained by sloping the pool rim and/or adjacent surfaces from a point at least 600 mm (2 ft) beyond the necessary clearance back toward the pool
sources.value: flush pool edge: slope rim/paving back toward the pool from >= 600 mm beyond the clearance
sources.note: Written for fountain pools (splash clearance): the margin returns splash and run-off to the pool. It does not address a person stepping into water; that is a GAP.

sources.document: Harris & Dines, Time-Saver Standards for Landscape Architecture
sources.quote: the hard-planted edge should have minimum freeboard of 75 mm (3 in), and the soft-planted edge made of loosely set cobbles, and gunite edges should extend to at least 150 mm (6 in) above the highest water level
sources.value: freeboard: hard-planted edge >= 75 mm; soft-planted / cobble edge >= 150 mm above highest water
sources.note: Freeboard is water level below the rim. For a flush pond it is the drop from ground to water.

sources.document: Harris & Dines, Time-Saver Standards for Landscape Architecture
sources.quote: The pool depth generally varies between 300 and 450 mm (12 and 18 in) . In the United States, 450 mm (18 in) is the maximum recommended depth because interpretation of the Uniform Building Code generally leads to the conclusion that anything of greater depth can be considered a swimming pool
sources.value: 300-450 mm: decorative/wading pool, US code reading
sources.note: NOT A KOI RULE. Recorded so nobody uses 450 mm as a koi depth or maximum: it is a fountain-pool figure tied to a US code reading. Koi depth is a GAP (GAP-POND-DEPTH).

sources.document: Harris & Dines, Time-Saver Standards for Landscape Architecture
sources.quote: Lawns 200-300 mm (8-12 in) Flowers and ground covers 250-300 mm (10-12 in) Shrubs 600-750 mm (24-30 in)t Small trees 750-1 050 mm (30-42 in) Large trees 1 500-1 800 mm (5-6 ft)
sources.value: min soil depth: lawn 200, ground cover 250, shrub 600, small tree 750, large tree 1 500 mm (lower bound of each range)
sources.note: Table is for roof and deck landscapes (planting medium on a filter blanket and drainage medium). Applied to planting over the basement slab and the top deck; the lower bound of each range is used.

sources.document: Harris & Dines, Time-Saver Standards for Landscape Architecture
sources.locator: p. 320-13, Table 320-2 Recommended Gradients: General (columns Maximum / Minimum / Preferred, %)
sources.quote: Concrete walks Longitudinal slope of sidewalks 10 0.5 1-5 Cross slope of sidewalks 4 1 2 Approaches, platforms, etc . 8 0.5 2 Service areas 10 0.5 2-3 Terrace and sitting areas Concrete 2 0.5 1 Flagstone, slate, brick 2 0.75 1 Lawn areas Recreation, games, etc . (noncompetitive) 5 1 2-3 Grassed athletic fields 2 0.5 1 Lawns and grass areas 25 1 5-10 Berms and mounds 20 5 10 Mowed slopes 25 (3 :1) 20 Unmowed grass banks Angle of repose 25 Planted slopes and beds 10 0.5 3-5
sources.value: terrace concrete 0.5-2 %, flagstone/slate/brick 0.75-2 %; walk cross slope 1-4 %; walk long. 0.5-10 %; recreation lawn 1-5 %; planted beds 0.5-10 %
sources.note: Row 'Terrace and sitting areas' is the paving-drainage figure for dining/lounge terraces.

sources.document: Harris & Dines, Time-Saver Standards for Landscape Architecture
sources.quote: Cross slopes on paths and ramps should not exceed 2% in developed areas
sources.value: accessible cross slope <= 2 % in developed areas
sources.note: Accessible routes; used for the main path only.

sources.document: Harris & Dines, Time-Saver Standards for Landscape Architecture
sources.locator: p. 750-11, sprinkler head selection and layout
sources.quote: divide the area to be irrigated into zones that have similar water requirements
sources.value: irrigation zones of similar water requirement
sources.note: Qualitative principle; the rule counts distinct water-need classes per planting group, so 'one class' is our operational reading (policy).

sources.document: Harris & Dines, Time-Saver Standards for Landscape Architecture
sources.quote: Use turf only where it is clearly serving a purpose such as play areas, sports fields, etc . 2 . Shape turf areas to allow maximum irrigation efficiency. The ratio of area to perimeter should be high . Do not use lawn in areas too small or narrow to be irrigated efficiently
sources.value: qualitative; no minimum width given
sources.note: No numeric minimum lawn width exists in this source (GAP-LAWN-WIDTH). Brief now allows lawn per area, so purpose must be stated.

sources.document: Harris & Dines, Time-Saver Standards for Landscape Architecture
sources.locator: p. 340-4, Visual Perception: Sense of Spatial Enclosure (Figure 340-10, p. 340-8)
sources.quote: An external enclosure is most comfortable when its vertical planes are one- half to one-third as high as the width of the space enclosed . If the ratio falls below one-fourth, the space begins to lack a sense of enclosure
sources.value: enclosing height / width >= 1:4 (comfortable 1:3 to 1:2)
sources.note: A perceptual figure; reported as a warning.

sources.document: Harris & Dines, Time-Saver Standards for Landscape Architecture
sources.quote: the root zone of a plant (the area within the dripline of the plant) is neither compacted nor covered with a material that would restrict the amount of air or moisture reaching the root zone
sources.value: root zone = area within the dripline; keep it uncovered and uncompacted
sources.note: Written for protecting existing plants during construction; applied to mature spread by analogy, so a warning. No tree-to-building distance in this book (GAP-TREE-BUILDING).

sources.document: Buxton (ed.), Metric Handbook: Planning and Design Data
sources.locator: p. 22-18, Houses and flats, enclosure of gardens
sources.quote: An impermeable wall or fence of approximately 1.8 m height is normally recommended at the far end. The side (party fence) enclosures can be reduced to approximately 1.2 m
sources.value: rear garden boundary ~1.8 m impermeable; side ~1.2 m
sources.note: UK suburban housing. The brief says privacy is critical, so ALL neighbour-facing boundaries use 1.8 m (policy: stricter than the source for sides). Overlooking from the apartment above is not solved by a boundary (GAP-OVERLOOK-ABOVE).

sources.document: Lechner & Andrasik, Heating, Cooling, Lighting
sources.locator: design-guideline list 'Use plants for shading' (EPUB-converted PDF index 378; chapter number not verified)
sources.quote: Evergreen trees can be used on the east, west, and north sides of a building. Deciduous plants are most appropriate for shading the southeast, the southwest, and the roof. Unless carefully placed, deciduous plants on the south side of a building might do more harm than good
sources.value: qualitative
sources.note: About shading a BUILDING for energy, true-compass sides (north-hemisphere). Advisory only; the client's 'south garden' is the model +x side and is not true south (CLAUDE.md orientation).

sources.document: Garden brief (client decision 2026-11-22)
sources.quote: gatherings and social events for ~10-20 people
sources.value: >= 10 seats (a dining group plus a lounge group)
sources.note: Client decision, not a published standard.

sources.document: Garden brief (client decision 2026-11-22)
sources.quote: Fire pit: clearance to the facade and to planting follows the product's instructions
sources.value: per product
sources.note: Client decision: no published number is invented.

sources.document: Garden brief (client decision 2026-11-22)
sources.quote: Privacy is critical: strong screening from the neighbours and from the apartment above
sources.value: all neighbour sides at the 1.8 m rear figure
sources.note: Policy tightening of MH-22-18 (side 1.2 m).

sources.document: Alexander, Ishikawa, Silverstein et al., A Pattern Language
sources.value: pattern number and name
sources.note: The book is NOT held on this machine (not in the knowledge index or the archpipe_books corpus; docs/guidance/coverage-and-acquisition.md lists it as an acquisition target). Pattern numbers and names are from the published contents; no passage was read, no page cited. Critics may cite number and name; they may not quote or paraphrase text from it until the book is held and read.

rules.title: Main path clear width
rules.fix: Widen the main path to 1 200 mm clear, or reclassify it as secondary if it carries one person at a time.

rules.title: Secondary path clear width (one person)
rules.fix: Widen the path to 600 mm clear (one pedestrian).

rules.title: Outdoor step riser
rules.fix: Re-divide the level change so every riser is 115-150 mm (175 mm only for a utilitarian step).

rules.title: Outdoor step relation 2R + G
rules.fix: Adjust the going so that 2 x riser + going is 650-675 mm.

rules.title: No single steps
rules.fix: Make the level change a ramp, or at least two (preferably three) steps announced by railing, planting or lighting; or remove it.

rules.title: Private stair width
rules.fix: Widen the stair to 1 050 mm.

rules.title: Rise between landings
rules.fix: Insert a landing so no flight rises more than 1 500 mm.

rules.title: Seat wall height and width
rules.fix: Bring the seat wall to 350-450 mm high and 400-450 mm wide.

rules.title: Dining zone area per seat
rules.reference: Time-Saver Landscape 2nd ed. p. 210-3, Fig. 210-3 (derived per seat)

params.basis: 4 200 mm dia. circle / 4 seats; (3.6 x 4.8 m with 1.2 m strip) / 4 seats

rules.fix: Enlarge the dining paving, or seat fewer people at it (3.46 m2 per seat; 4.32 m2 where circulation runs along one side).

rules.title: Clear strip around a dining table
rules.reference: Time-Saver Landscape 2nd ed. Fig. 210-3; Time-Saver Interior 2nd ed. p. 268
rules.fix: Move the table, or the planting/wall/feature, so 1 200 mm stays clear from the table edge on all sides. Conservative: the figure shows the strip on one side only.

rules.title: Seats for the briefed group
rules.fix: Add seating (a lounge group) until at least 10 people sit; standing room for the rest is a GAP.

rules.title: Clear level ground around a fire pit or BBQ
rules.layout: features[kind in firepit,bbq] against obstacles, buildings, planting
rules.fix: Keep 900 mm (1 200 mm recommended) of clear level hard ground on every side of the pit or BBQ stand.

rules.title: Fire ring to nearest seated person
rules.fix: Move the seating back to 1 500 mm from the fire, or confirm the pit is small enough for the shorter distance (the source figure is for a >= 1 800 mm ring).

rules.title: Fire pit / BBQ clearance to facade and planting declared from the product
rules.fix: Enter the manufacturer's clearance for the chosen product; the check then compares it with the layout. Until then it is not_evaluated.

rules.title: Flush fire pit cover: load rating declared
rules.reference: Client brief addendum 2026-11-22 (flush, concealed); no published figure held
rules.fix: Obtain the cover's load rating from the supplier. No required value is held (GAP-FIRE-COVER-LOAD): a declared rating is reported as a warning, never a pass.

rules.title: Pond edge freeboard (water below the rim)
rules.fix: Lower the water level (or raise the rim) to the freeboard for the edge type.

rules.title: Flush pond: paving sloped back toward the pond
rules.fix: Slope the rim or the adjacent paving back toward the pond from at least 600 mm beyond the splash clearance.

rules.title: Soil depth for planting over structure
rules.fix: Deepen the planter or raise the bed to the depth for the plant form, or change the plant form.

rules.title: Fall of paving, paths, lawn and beds
rules.reference: Time-Saver Landscape 2nd ed. p. 320-13 Table 320-2; p. 240-8
rules.fix: Re-grade: terraces 0.5-2 % (1 % preferred), walks 1-4 % cross fall, recreation lawn 1-5 %.

rules.title: One water-need class per planting group
rules.fix: Regroup plants so each irrigation group has one water-need class (swap species, or split the bed).

rules.title: Sense of enclosure of an outdoor room
rules.layout: zones[use in dining,lounge,quiet].enclosure_height_m / min rect side
rules.fix: Raise the enclosing wall, screen or planting, or reduce the width of the room, until height : width reaches 1:4.

rules.title: Neighbour-side boundary height
rules.reference: Metric Handbook 7th ed. p. 22-18; client brief (privacy critical)
rules.fix: Raise the wall or fence to 1.8 m (a hedge: stated mature height and density; hedge density is a GAP).

rules.title: Mature tree root zone not covered by paving or buildings
rules.fix: Keep paving and buildings out of the dripline, use permeable surfacing there, or move the tree.

advisory.title: Positive Outdoor Space
advisory.reference: Alexander, A Pattern Language, 106 Positive Outdoor Space
advisory.prompt: Is each outdoor area shaped as a positive space (like a room with its own boundary) rather than left over between the building and the edge?

advisory.title: Outdoor Room
advisory.reference: Alexander, A Pattern Language, 163 Outdoor Room
advisory.prompt: Does the dining or lounge group read as a room with a back, a floor and a partial roof (pergola/canopy), rather than furniture on open paving?

advisory.title: Hierarchy of Open Space
advisory.reference: Alexander, A Pattern Language, 114 Hierarchy of Open Space
advisory.prompt: Is there a graded sequence from the open social space to the semi-private to the private quiet corner?

advisory.title: South Facing Outdoors
advisory.reference: Alexander, A Pattern Language, 105 South Facing Outdoors
advisory.prompt: Is the main outdoor use area on the sunny side of the building in winter (true south is the sun direction; the client's 'south garden' is model +x)? Pattern written for a temperate climate: weigh against the brief's 'shade over sun' in the Cairo summer.

advisory.title: Half-Hidden Garden
advisory.reference: Alexander, A Pattern Language, 111 Half-Hidden Garden
advisory.prompt: Is the quiet corner half-hidden, visible but not exposed, and reached by a route that does not cross the social area?

advisory.title: Quiet Backs
advisory.reference: Alexander, A Pattern Language, 59 Quiet Backs
advisory.prompt: Does the quiet garden sit on the quiet side of the site, away from the street and the gathering area?

advisory.title: Tree Places
advisory.reference: Alexander, A Pattern Language, 171 Tree Places
advisory.prompt: Is each shade tree placed where people will gather under it, with a place to sit?

advisory.title: Garden Seat
advisory.reference: Alexander, A Pattern Language, 176 Garden Seat
advisory.prompt: Is there a seat at the quiet edge of the garden, in a spot that is sunny or shaded to suit the season of use?

advisory.title: Garden Growing Wild
advisory.reference: Alexander, A Pattern Language, 172 Garden Growing Wild
advisory.prompt: Does a part of the garden (the lush tropical/Japanese planting) grow loose and layered rather than clipped and bedded?

advisory.title: Pools and Streams
advisory.reference: Alexander, A Pattern Language, 64 Pools and Streams
advisory.prompt: Is the water reachable and part of the daily route, not a showpiece behind a barrier? (Client: pond discreet, within the planting.)

advisory.title: Still Water
advisory.reference: Alexander, A Pattern Language, 71 Still Water
advisory.prompt: Does the still water give the quiet corner a focus that draws people to sit by it?

advisory.title: Activity Pockets
advisory.reference: Alexander, A Pattern Language, 124 Activity Pockets
advisory.prompt: Are there small pockets of activity (fire pit circle, BBQ corner, herb bed) around the edge of the main space, not in the middle of it?

advisory.title: Something Roughly in the Middle
advisory.reference: Alexander, A Pattern Language, 126 Something Roughly in the Middle
advisory.prompt: Does the gathering space have a roughly central draw (fire, table, tree) that people gather round?

advisory.title: Garden Wall
advisory.reference: Alexander, A Pattern Language, 173 Garden Wall
advisory.prompt: Are the boundary walls part of the garden (planted, seated against, climbed) rather than bare fences?

advisory.title: Climbing Plants
advisory.reference: Alexander, A Pattern Language, 246 Climbing Plants
advisory.prompt: Are climbers used on walls, pergolas and trellis to add height and screening?

advisory.title: Trellised Walk
advisory.reference: Alexander, A Pattern Language, 174 Trellised Walk
advisory.prompt: Does a path between the gardens pass under a trellis or planted cover so that the transition is felt?

advisory.title: Vegetable Garden
advisory.reference: Alexander, A Pattern Language, 177 Vegetable Garden
advisory.prompt: Is the herb/fruit bed close to the kitchen door and in the sun, so it is used every day?

advisory.title: Fruit Trees
advisory.reference: Alexander, A Pattern Language, 170 Fruit Trees
advisory.prompt: Are fruit trees placed where people pass and can pick, as part of the garden rather than a separate orchard?

advisory.title: Paths and Goals
advisory.reference: Alexander, A Pattern Language, 120 Paths and Goals
advisory.prompt: Does each path run to a real destination and follow the line people would walk?

advisory.title: Path Shape
advisory.reference: Alexander, A Pattern Language, 121 Path Shape
advisory.prompt: Are the paths wide at the places people stop and narrow where they pass, with room to linger at the edges?

advisory.title: Stair Seats
advisory.reference: Alexander, A Pattern Language, 125 Stair Seats
advisory.prompt: Do level changes and low walls double as seating where people gather?

advisory.title: Seat Spots
advisory.reference: Alexander, A Pattern Language, 241 Seat Spots
advisory.prompt: Are there places to sit at the edges of the space with a view of the activity and a back to a wall or planting?

advisory.title: Raised Flowers
advisory.reference: Alexander, A Pattern Language, 245 Raised Flowers
advisory.prompt: Are colourful drifts raised or brought to eye/hand height where they will be looked at and touched?

advisory.title: Paving with Cracks Between the Stones
advisory.reference: Alexander, A Pattern Language, 247 Paving with Cracks Between the Stones
advisory.prompt: Does the paving let plants and water soak through, tying the paving to the planting?

advisory.title: Connection to the Earth
advisory.reference: Alexander, A Pattern Language, 168 Connection to the Earth
advisory.prompt: Does the terrace step down gently to the ground so the house and garden are connected?

advisory.title: Site Repair
advisory.reference: Alexander, A Pattern Language, 104 Site Repair
advisory.prompt: Does the layout build on the best parts of the site (existing shade, view, level) and leave the worst for service?

advisory.title: Accessible Green
advisory.reference: Alexander, A Pattern Language, 60 Accessible Green
advisory.prompt: Is green space reachable from the indoor rooms the family uses, by an obvious short route?

advisory.title: Floor, wall and canopy make the outdoor room
advisory.reference: Time-Saver Landscape 2nd ed. p. 210-2, Fig. 210-1 'Elements of spatial enclosure: floor, wall, canopy, modified by time, light, climate, and intensity of activity'
advisory.prompt: Does each outdoor room have a defined floor, walls (screen, planting) and a canopy (tree, pergola)? The numeric 1:4 limit is the quantitative rule LS-ENCLOSURE; this prompt is the qualitative side.

advisory.title: Pond edge to suit a naturalistic setting
advisory.reference: Time-Saver Landscape 2nd ed. p. 530-11 (Setting) and p. 530-15 (edge conditions)
advisory.prompt: Time-Saver: a naturalistic setting directs the design toward 'organic shapes, soft edges'; an at-grade water level 'will integrate the pool into the surrounding plane'; a soft-planted edge 'is usually employed in ... naturalistic streams, ponds'. Does the pond edge match the lush tropical/Japanese character and the flush brief, and is the edge still legible as a water edge?

advisory.title: Stair rhythm suits the place
advisory.reference: Time-Saver Landscape 2nd ed. p. 340-8, Additional Considerations 2
advisory.prompt: Is the stair's kinesthetic character congruent with the garden's character (Time-Saver: 'the sense of rhythm to be experienced by the pedestrian')?

advisory.title: Level changes announced
advisory.reference: Time-Saver Landscape 2nd ed. p. 340-8, Additional Considerations 3
advisory.prompt: Is every level change, and every flush hazard edge, announced by railing, planting or lighting?
advisory.applies_to: steps, flush pond, flush fire pit

advisory.title: Lawn only where it serves a purpose
advisory.reference: Time-Saver Landscape 2nd ed. p. 550-14 Practical Turf Areas
advisory.prompt: Does each lawn area have a stated purpose, a compact shape (high area-to-perimeter ratio), and no narrow strips or hard-to-irrigate slopes? (No numeric minimum width held: GAP-LAWN-WIDTH.)

advisory.title: Lush planting without heavy irrigation
advisory.reference: Time-Saver Landscape 2nd ed. p. 550-14 Planning and Design
advisory.prompt: Time-Saver: 'Xeriscape gardens do not have to be spare and bare; drought-tolerant plants can look lush without heavy irrigation.' Does the planting plan get the lush tropical/Japanese look from plants that suit the site, with irrigation concentrated where it is needed?

advisory.title: Deciduous or evergreen shade by compass side
advisory.reference: Lechner, Heating Cooling Lighting 5th ed. 2021, design guideline 'Use plants for shading'
advisory.prompt: For shade over the use areas and the facade, are trees chosen by the side they shade (true compass), noting Lechner's warning on the south side of a building? Qualitative: no shade percentage is held (GAP-SHADE-TARGET).

gaps.item: Service path width (bins, wheelbarrow, maintenance access)
gaps.closest: TS 340-11: one-way accessible clear width 900 mm (ramp); Neufert 1980 garden equipment (wheelbarrow, mower dimensions, p.107) gives equipment size, not a path width
gaps.needed: a published service-path or equipment-access width
gaps.interim: none; LS-PATH-* skip class=service and report not_evaluated

gaps.item: Terrace area per person for a lounge group (and standing room)
gaps.searched: Time-Saver Landscape, Time-Saver Interior, Metric Handbook, Neufert 1980
gaps.closest: TS 210-3 dining only; Neufert 1980 p. 107 garden chair and table sizes
gaps.needed: a per-person lounge or standing-gathering area figure
gaps.interim: LS-CAPACITY counts seats against the brief (policy) and LS-DINE-AREA covers dining; lounge and standing area are advisory (AD-APL-163/124) until sourced

gaps.item: Fire pit / BBQ safe distance to combustible facade and planting
gaps.searched: Time-Saver Landscape, UK Approved Document B
gaps.closest: TS 240-19 and 520-24 give ground space and seating distance, not safe distance to combustibles
gaps.interim: LS-FIRE-PRODUCT is not_evaluated until the product clearance is entered

gaps.item: Flush fire pit cover: required load rating, fall and burn protection
gaps.searched: Time-Saver Landscape, UK Approved Documents K and B, ADA 2010
gaps.needed: supplier rating and a standard for a loaded flush cover
gaps.interim: LS-FIRE-COVER reports a declared rating as a warning only

gaps.closest: TS 530-15: 300-450 mm is a decorative/wading-pool depth with a US code reading (card TS-530-15-depth-NOT-KOI); it must NOT be used as koi depth
gaps.needed: koi-keeping source; the brief assigns filtration, depth and liner to a pond supplier
gaps.interim: none; the layout carries volume_m3 and depth_mm for the supplier, unchecked

gaps.item: Flush pond: edge visibility, contrasting margin, safety shelf, night lighting of edges
gaps.searched: Time-Saver Landscape (530, 240, 340), UK Approved Document K, ADA 2010
gaps.closest: TS 340-8 item 3 (announce single steps by railing, planting or lighting): advisory AD-TS-STEP-ANNOUNCE; TS 530-15 margin slope (LS-POND-FLUSH-MARGIN) addresses splash, not a stepping-in fall
gaps.needed: a source for edge contrast, shelf width and edge-lighting level
gaps.interim: advisory prompt only; lighting handed to lighting lanes without a target

gaps.item: Pond distance to trees (leaf fall), sun/shade on the water
